lesson.title: One Kinase Calls the Next: The Logic of Signaling Cascades
lesson.summary: A phosphorylation cascade is a chain of protein kinases in which each activated kinase phosphorylates and activates the next kinase in line, a mechanism used by both receptor tyrosine kinases and second messenger pathways to convert a brief signal into a strong, sustained, and reversible cellular response.
lesson.body:
A single phosphorylation event, one kinase adding a phosphate group to one target protein, is a useful but limited tool on its own. Its real power in cell signaling comes from being chained together into a phosphorylation cascade, a sequence in which an activated kinase phosphorylates and activates a second kinase, which phosphorylates and activates a third, and so on, before finally phosphorylating a non-kinase target protein that carries out the actual cellular response. This chaining is possible because phosphorylation, the attachment of a negatively charged phosphate group from ATP onto a serine, threonine, or tyrosine residue, reliably changes a target protein's three dimensional shape and can either switch an enzyme on or switch it off depending on where the phosphate lands.

The RAS-MAPK cascade downstream of activated receptor tyrosine kinases is the clearest example of this architecture. Ligand binding causes an RTK to dimerize and autophosphorylate, creating docking sites that recruit and activate the small G protein RAS. Active RAS then activates a first kinase, often called RAF, which phosphorylates and activates a second kinase, MEK, which in turn phosphorylates and activates a third kinase, ERK, also known as MAPK. Only at this final tier does the cascade reach targets outside the kinase chain itself, since active ERK can phosphorylate transcription factors in the nucleus and other cytoplasmic proteins that together drive processes such as cell growth and division.

Cascades are not unique to receptor tyrosine kinases. The cyclic AMP pathway covered in the previous section is also a short phosphorylation cascade: protein kinase A phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase kinase, which phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase. Both the RTK triggered cascade and the second messenger triggered cascade rely on the same underlying chemistry, an enzyme that uses ATP to add phosphate groups to specific residues on its target, and both use the resulting shape change to switch each downstream enzyme between active and inactive states.

Building a response out of a multi-step chain rather than a single reaction gives the cell several advantages. Each tier in the cascade is a point where the signal can be regulated, boosted by a different input pathway, or shut down by a phosphatase, so cascades allow different signaling pathways to be integrated with one another rather than running in complete isolation. A multi-step chain also introduces a short delay and a threshold like quality, since a cascade often needs a certain minimum level of activation to propagate all the way through, which helps prevent the cell from overreacting to background noise or a single stray signaling molecule.

Every kinase in a cascade is opposed by a corresponding phosphatase enzyme that removes the phosphate group it added, and this balance between kinases adding phosphates and phosphatases removing them is what determines whether a pathway stays on, turns off quickly, or oscillates, rather than the kinases alone. Because each kinase in the chain is a catalyst capable of activating many copies of the next kinase before it is itself switched off, phosphorylation cascades are also the primary engine behind the dramatic signal amplification described in the next section, where a small number of receptor binding events at the cell membrane can ultimately affect a very large number of target molecules deep inside the cell.
